title: Seabirds, forests, and coral could help save sinking islands
gist: A Science Advances study of 28 atoll islands in the Pacific and Indian oceans found that rat-free islands with abundant seabirds and native vegetation have roughly twice the reef accretion potential, enough to keep pace with sea-level rise to 2100 at about 2 C of warming. Authors caution it is not a miracle fix and emissions cuts remain essential.

insights.claim: Seabirds move nutrients from the open ocean onto atolls as guano, which feeds land plants, marine life and coral growth, and islands with greater seabird nutrient input tended to have more productive coral communities and higher energy flow.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Ecosystem health, not just structures, can determine whether atolls keep pace with sea level.

insights.claim: Reef accretion potential was twice as high on lagoonal and ocean-facing reefs around rat-free islands with abundant seabirds as around rat-infested islands, sufficient to closely keep up with predicted sea-level rise to the end of the century under a 2 C warming scenario.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Quantified benefit supports funding for invasive-species eradication as climate adaptation.
insights.quote: sufficient to closely keep up with predicted sea-level rises to the end of the century
insights.locator: The new study measures the “reef accretion potential”

insights.claim: Parrotfish and other reef feeders turn dead coral into sand that maintains beaches, and calcifying algae, other reef organisms and shellfish build the reef framework upward to buffer islands from waves.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Reef biology provides the sediment supply; protecting these species is part of the resilience mechanism.

themes.theme: Restoration levers: rats and coconut plantations

insights.claim: Eradicating invasive rats and replacing coconut plantations with native forests and brush could give some atolls a fighting chance to persist at the sea-level rise expected late this century with about 2 C of warming.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Low-cost interventions are targets for conservation finance and climate-adaptation programs.
insights.locator: Eradicating rats and replacing coconut plantations

insights.claim: Coconut palms have small, unstable rootballs that leave soil vulnerable to erosion, while native plants have fine, extensive root networks that stabilize shallow porous soil and provide better seabird habitat.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Plantation economics collide with island stability; land-use change is a key lever.
insights.locator: In the terrestrial part of the cycle

insights.claim: Invasive rats brought by colonizers have devastated seabird colonies for centuries, and the seabird-nutrient cycle has sustained atoll ecosystems at least since the end of the last ice age.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Human-introduced pests broke a long-running natural adaptation system.

insights.claim: The study did not make direct before-and-after restoration comparisons and used islands with differing seabird abundance and rat infestation, differences the team tried to smooth with an ecosystem energetics framework.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Evidence is correlational, so treat outcomes as indicative rather than guaranteed.

insights.claim: Reef accretion does not necessarily mean an atoll is growing vertically, because warming also changes waves, winds and currents that determine where material ends up, and a 2026 study of 288 reef core records found most kept pace with sea-level rise but not guaranteed at the current warming rate.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Physical outcomes vary by location, limiting extrapolation.

insights.claim: The study focused on mostly uninhabited or sparsely populated islands, and on developed atolls restoration can help but will not replace the need for engineering solutions.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Inhabited atolls still need engineered defenses, so nature-based and hard infrastructure are complements.

insights.claim: Local conservation can influence physical resilience to rising seas, but rapid reductions in greenhouse-gas emissions remain essential to the long-term viability of these systems, and the fate of an atoll cannot be managed by treating land and sea separately.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Adaptation is not a substitute for mitigation.
insights.quote: rapid reductions in greenhouse-gas emissions remain essential to long-­term viability of these systems

insights.claim: Nature restoration buffers climate impacts more broadly: restoring wetlands and forests dampens swings between wet and dry spells, reducing flood and fire hazards, and can slow warming by supporting natural carbon storage.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Supports the case for nature-based solutions in adaptation and carbon policy.
